findings.who: An itemizing filer who deducts Schedule A mortgage interest on a condominium or house rented out for short stays (transient basis) and has no boat or camper interest, where adding that short-stay home interest to AMTI is what makes line 7 exceed line 10.
findings.why_no: The computed gate helper adds only private activity bond interest and boat or camper mortgage interest at their largest. It does not add short-stay/transient home mortgage interest, so the tool computes the gate false, never asks s2.amt_boat, and silently treats s2.amt_boat_if_could as zero.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 8, Line 3, Mortgage Interest: If you deducted home mortgage interest on Schedule A for a dwelling that isn’t a principal residence or qualified dwelling for AMT, include that deducted interest on line 3. A qualified dwelling for AMT is a house, apartment, condominium, or mobile home not used on a transient basis.
findings.fix: Broaden the gate helper to add all nonqualified-dwelling mortgage interest at its largest, including short-stay/transient house, apartment, condominium, or mobile-home interest, or ask the gated question whenever Schedule A home mortgage interest is positive and AMT could apply after adding any such interest.

findings.who: An itemizing filer with a second condominium or house used for short stays by family or guests but not rented out, who deducts the mortgage interest on Schedule A and where adding that interest could make AMT apply.
findings.why_no: The question asks only about a home rented out for short stays. The filer reads their non-rented short-stay use as outside that phrase and answers no, although the IRS text refers more broadly to a house, apartment, condominium, or mobile home used on a transient basis.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 8, Line 3, Mortgage Interest: A qualified dwelling for AMT is a house, apartment, condominium, or mobile home not used on a transient basis; include deducted interest for a dwelling that isn’t a principal residence or qualified dwelling for AMT on line 3.
findings.fix: Use the statutory phrase used on a transient basis and give examples, including short-stay rentals, rather than limiting the question to a home rented out for short stays.

findings.who: A filer (or spouse) whose only tax-exempt income is exempt-interest dividends from a municipal bond mutual fund or ETF. The fund reports part of those dividends as specified private activity bond interest dividends on Form 1099-DIV.
findings.why_no: The question has them add only box 9 of Forms 1099-INT and box 11 of Form 1099-OID, and ends 'Zero if none.' They have no 1099-INT box 9 and no 1099-OID, so they truthfully enter zero. The help covers only those two forms.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 3, Line 2g: 'Exempt-interest dividends paid by a mutual fund or other regulated investment company are treated as interest income'; i1099int p. 1: 'Report exempt-interest dividends from a mutual fund or other regulated investment company (RIC) on Form 1099-DIV.'
findings.fix: Add 'plus the private activity bond part of exempt-interest dividends from mutual funds or ETFs (Form 1099-DIV, the specified private activity bond interest dividends box, which is part of the exempt-interest dividends box).' Also confirm that the gate's tax-exempt interest helper includes exempt-interest dividends, so the question is reached.

findings.who: A filer who holds a private activity bond directly and received less than $10 of tax-exempt interest, or whose payer did not issue a Form 1099-INT. Examples are a privately placed bond or a payer that is excused from reporting.
findings.why_no: The question has them add up box 9 of their Forms 1099-INT. With no form, the sum is zero, and the question says 'Zero if none.' The instructions say a payer 'should' send a form, but the amount counts whether or not a form arrives.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 3: 'Enter on line 2g interest income from "specified private activity bonds"... Each payer of this type of interest should send you a Form 1099-INT'; i1099int p. 1: File Form 1099-INT for 'amounts reportable in boxes 1, 3, or 8 of at least $10'
findings.fix: Ask for the fact rather than the form: 'How much tax-exempt interest did you or your spouse get from private activity bonds? This is usually in box 9 of Form 1099-INT, but include it even if you got no form.'

findings.who: A partner or S corporation shareholder (or spouse) whose Schedule K-1 passes through tax-exempt interest that includes private activity bond interest. The K-1 shows it as a tax-exempt or AMT item, not on a Form 1099.
findings.why_no: The question names only Forms 1099-INT and 1099-OID, so a filer whose only private activity bond interest comes on a K-1 enters zero.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 3: 'Enter on line 2g interest income from "specified private activity bonds"'; f6251 line 2g: 'Interest from specified private activity bonds exempt from the regular tax'
findings.fix: Add 'and any private activity bond interest shown on a Schedule K-1 from a partnership or S corporation.' Estate and trust K-1 amounts already go to line 2j. Also make sure the gate's tax-exempt interest helper counts K-1 tax-exempt interest.

findings.who: A filer whose amortized bond premium on tax-exempt bonds (Form 1099-INT box 13) equals or exceeds the tax-exempt interest on some bonds. The bonds include private activity bonds, and the filer has other tax-exempt interest that is not private activity bond interest.
findings.why_no: The gate tests tax-exempt interest 'net of amortized premium.' Depending on how the netting is aggregated, the net can reach zero or be understated even though some box 9 interest remains. In that case the gate never asks the question.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 3: 'interest income from "specified private activity bonds" reduced (but not below zero) by any deduction that would have been allowable if the interest were includible in gross income'
findings.fix: Open the gate when gross tax-exempt interest (1099-INT box 8, 1099-OID box 11, exempt-interest dividends, K-1 tax-exempt interest) is above zero, before any premium is netted.

findings.who: A couple paid a caretaker or housekeeper $4,000 in 2025 to look after their vacation cabin or second home. They paid no one at their main residence.
findings.why_no: "Work in or around your home" reads as the main residence. The examples (nanny, carer, housekeeper, gardener) and the help never say that a second home, vacation home or other private residence counts.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 (2025) p.1, line 9: "Household employment taxes. Attach Schedule H". Schedule H covers household work done in or around your private home, and that includes any residence you keep.
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Count work at any home you or your spouse own or rent, including a vacation home or second home."

findings.who: A filer paid an adult sister, or a niece aged 22, $300 a week through 2025 to care for the filer's children or an ill spouse in the filer's home.
findings.why_no: The filer thinks of money given to a relative for helping out as family support, not as paying "anyone to work". The examples are all job titles (nanny, housekeeper), so a relative does not seem to fit.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 (2025) p.1, line 9: "Household employment taxes. Attach Schedule H". Under Schedule H, a relative other than your spouse, your child under 21 or (generally) your parent is a household employee like anyone else.
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Count relatives you paid, such as a sibling, grandchild, niece or adult child. The next question sets aside your spouse, your child under 21, and in most cases your parent."

findings.who: A filer paid a full-time private chef, personal assistant, tutor, or caretaker of the filer's animals who worked at the filer's home in 2025.
findings.why_no: The examples (nanny, carer, housekeeper, gardener, plus a driver in the help) read as the complete list of household roles, so a cook, a tutor or an animal caretaker seems not to count.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 (2025) p.1, line 9: "Household employment taxes. Attach Schedule H". The Schedule H list of household workers includes cooks, caretakers and private nurses, and it is not limited to those roles.
findings.fix: Change "such as" to "anyone who works under your direction in or around your home, for example a nanny, babysitter, carer, cook, housekeeper, gardener, caretaker, tutor or driver".

findings.who: A 17-year-old who is not in school worked full-time as the filer's live-in nanny in 2025 and was paid $15,000.
findings.why_no: This is a misreading of the gated question's help, not of the gate. The help's "leave out a student under 18" may be read as "leave out anyone under 18". The help also omits the rule that a minor whose principal occupation is household work still counts toward the $2,800 test.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 (2025) p.1, line 9: "Household employment taxes. Attach Schedule H". Schedule H leaves out wages paid to an employee under 18 only if household work is not that employee's principal occupation.
findings.fix: Reword: "For the $2,800 test only, leave out a worker under 18 for whom household work is not their main occupation (for example a student). Count a minor for whom it is."

locators: Schedule 2 (2025), line 9, "Household employment taxes. Attach Schedule H"

findings.who: A small commercial remodeling contractor on Schedule C uses the completed-contract method for regular tax, as section 460(e)(1)(B) allows. The contractor never files Form 6251 or works out income as the job progresses, and a multi-year contract finished in 2025.
findings.why_no: The question asks about a contract 'with its income figured as the work went on'. This filer never figured it that way. The help sentence 'Count a contract whose income was figured as the work went on for the alternative minimum tax only' describes a computation that was never made, so the filer answers No. 'If neither is familiar, answer No' supports that answer.
findings.line: s2.lookback_if_business (Schedule 2 line 17n; a Yes should end the interview, so the refusal is missed)
findings.irs_text: i6251 (2025) p. 7, Line 2p: 'For the AMT, you must generally use the percentage-of-completion method ... If you are required to use the percentage-of-completion method for either the regular tax or the AMT, you may owe or be entitled to a refund of interest for the tax year the contract is completed or adjusted.'
findings.fix: Ask about the fact the filer can check, then classify: 'Did you (or your spouse) have a contract to build, install, make or manufacture something that began in one tax year and was finished, or had its price or costs changed, in 2025? Answer Yes even if you report the income only when the job is done, unless it is a contract to build or improve homes (or other dwellings of 4 or fewer units).'

findings.who: A married filer owns 40% of a closely held partnership or S corporation that has a multi-year construction contract finished in 2025. The owner's share of the look-back interest is figured on the owner's own Form 8697 from Schedule K-1 information.
findings.why_no: The question reads 'Did you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) have a contract'. The contract belongs to the entity, not the filer personally. The filer also cannot see the entity's accounting method.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 Schedule 2 (2025) p. 2, line 17n: 'Look-back interest under section 167(g) or 460(b) from Form 8697 or 8866'
findings.fix: Add: 'including a contract or property of a partnership, S corporation, estate or trust in which you hold a share; check your Schedule K-1 for look-back (Form 8697 or 8866) information.'

findings.who: A filer reports no Schedule C and no 2025 royalties. The filer holds film or music rights as an investment and depreciates them under the income forecast method, and 2025 is the third recomputation year. The rights earned nothing in 2025, or were sold in 2025 with the gain reported on Form 8949.
findings.why_no: The computed gate is false. No Schedule C is filed and no royalty is listed in 2025. The filer also truthfully says no to having owned 'a business, a farm, a rental property, or a share of a partnership or an S corporation', because investment rights to a film are none of these. The question is never asked.
findings.line: s2.lookback_if_business (Schedule 2 line 17n; Form 8866 amount and refusal missed)
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 Schedule 2 (2025) p. 2, line 17n: 'Look-back interest under section 167(g) ... from Form 8697 or 8866'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate's scope question: 'In any year before 2025, did you (or your spouse) own a business, farm, rental, royalty-producing property (such as a film, book, recording or patent), or a share of a partnership or S corporation?' Alternatively, also trigger the gate on any depreciation or amortization reported, or on a 2025 sale of such property.

findings.who: A filer first acquired a partnership or S corporation interest in 2025, by purchase or gift, and reports it only on Schedule E with no Schedule C or royalties. The entity's long-term contract or income-forecast property passes a look-back computation through to owners in 2025.
findings.why_no: The scope question asks only about ownership 'In any year before 2025'. A 2025-only owner truthfully answers No, so the gate is false and the question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 Schedule 2 (2025) p. 2, line 17n: 'Look-back interest under section 167(g) or 460(b) from Form 8697 or 8866'
findings.fix: Also open the gate when the return reports any 2025 Schedule E partnership or S corporation income or Schedule F/Form 4835 activity: '... owned ... before or during 2025'.

used.revision: 2025 (the revision for tax year 2025, archived from irs-prior after irs.gov posted a later revision)
locators: p. 7, Line 2p, "you may owe or be entitled to a refund of interest for the tax year the contract is completed or adjusted"; f1040s2 Schedule 2 (2025), line 17n, "Look-back interest under section 167(g) or 460(b) from Form 8697 or 8866"

findings.who: A filer exercised an ISO before 2025 but the acquired shares stayed subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture until 2025, and the filer still held them at the end of 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only whether they used employee stock options to buy shares in 2025; they bought the shares in the earlier exercise year, so they truthfully answer no. The ISO helper also asks only about ISOs exercised in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 4, Line 2i: include on line 2i the excess of the fair market value of the stock acquired through exercise of the option when rights first become transferable or are no longer subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture over the amount paid.
findings.fix: Broaden the gate and ISO helper to ask whether in 2025 the filer exercised an ISO or had ISO stock first become transferable or no longer subject to forfeiture, and still held ISO shares at year-end.

findings.who: A filer whose ISO or ESPP shares bought through options in an earlier year were disposed of in 2025 in a merger, exchange, redemption, or gift rather than a sale, and the employer did not report the ordinary income in W-2 box 1.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only whether they sell shares bought that way. They did not sell, so they answer no, even though a disqualifying disposition can create income not otherwise reported.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 4, Line 2k: ordinary income from the disposition of property, such as a disqualifying disposition of stock acquired in a prior year by exercising an incentive stock option; i1040gi p. 91, line 8k: Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported.
findings.fix: Ask whether the filer sold or otherwise disposed of shares acquired through employee stock options or an ESPP, including disqualifying dispositions.

findings.who: A consultant or other non-employee service provider exercised nonqualified stock options in 2025 and had income not reported in W-2 box 1 and not otherwise reported on the return.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about employee stock options. The filer was not an employee and did not receive employee stock options, so answers no; the Schedule 1 line 8k instruction is not limited to employee options.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, line 8k: Stock options. Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1h.
findings.fix: Remove employee from the gate or add including stock options received for services as a non-employee; or add a separate line for non-employee stock options.

findings.who: A filer exercised an ISO in 2025 to buy shares that were restricted or vesting, still held them at the end of 2025, and either the shares vested in 2025 or the filer made a timely 83(b) election.
findings.why_no: The help says shares simply granted, such as restricted stock, do not count. The filer reads that as excluding their restricted ISO shares and answers no, even though the shares were acquired by exercising an ISO.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 4, Line 2i: the AMT adjustment applies to stock acquired through exercise of the option, including when rights are subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture or the filer makes the 30-day election.
findings.fix: Clarify that restricted stock acquired by exercising an option counts; only shares merely granted without an option are excluded.

findings.who: A filer did a cashless or net exercise of employee stock options in 2025, with income not reported in W-2 box 1: the broker exercised the options and immediately sold the shares, and the filer never held a share position.
findings.why_no: The filer reads use employee stock options to buy shares as requiring an actual purchase of shares and answers no, not treating the same-day exercise-and-sale as buying and selling shares.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, line 8k: Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported.
findings.fix: Say exercise employee stock options, including cashless or same-day exercise-and-sale, or sell shares acquired that way.

findings.who: A filer received employee stock options by gift, not by inheritance or divorce, from the employee; the filer exercised them in 2025 and had income not reported in W-2 box 1.
findings.why_no: The help says to count options that you inherited or got in a divorce. The filer did neither, reads the list as exhaustive, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, line 8k: Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported.
findings.fix: Say including options acquired by inheritance, divorce, gift, or other transfer, or simply options originally granted to any employee even if you were not the employee.

locators: p. 91, Line 8k, "Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1h"
